articles.title: Puzzles, People, and Publications: Measuring Shared Significance in Crosswords from 1942 to 2024
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.26677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Crossword puzzles are cultural objects that encode shared significance. We use interpretable, large-scale computational methods to analyze how crossword constructors, editors, and publications have adopted and adapted language to convey significance. Focusing on approximately 2.4 million crossword clue/answer pairs published in The New York Times between 1942 and 2024, we find shifting significance and differing editorial practices to be quantitatively measurable. articles.title: The Illusion of Evaluation: Challenges in Agentic Product Evaluation Practice
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.26923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic products introduce risks that extend beyond those of their underlying models, arising from their tools, permissions, data access, safeguards, and operating conditions. Existing evaluation instruments provide useful evidence about model behavior and agents in defined harnesses, but their results do not necessarily transfer to deployed products or cover risks created by product configurations and interactions. articles.summary: arXiv:2611.27005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We examined the association between submission of an assessment by day 30 and final course outcome in the Open University Learning Analytics Dataset (OULAD). To avoid classifying students who withdrew during the exposure window as comparable non-submitters, the main analysis was restricted to students enrolled at a day-30 landmark. articles.title: A Footprint-Sensitive Cross-GPU Timing Channel Through the Shared Host Memory Subsystem
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.27115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Assigning tenants to separate GPUs does not isolate their host memory traffic. We identify an unprivileged timing channel between GPUs without NVLink: a co-tenant can detect contention by timing reads to its own pinned host buffer, without accessing victim data or using hardware performance counters. The signal tracks the number of distinct host pages the victim touches rather than its throughput. articles.title: A Frugal AI Framework for India: Responsible and Right-sized AI
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.27189v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: India's AI debate often swings between two insufficient options: replicating the compute-intensive, capital-heavy foundation-model programmes of the United States or China, or remaining a downstream adopter of foreign AI with localised interfaces and safeguards. Neither serves a country that must deliver AI to a very large, diverse population across uneven infrastructure and within constrained budgets. articles.title: Answering the persona, not the person: Over-determination in the construction of synthetic respondents
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.27449v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Persona-prompted large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as synthetic survey respondents and digital twins. We examine how LLMs generate individual survey responses and why synthetic responses can show algorithmic fidelity in aggregate while tracking individual respondents poorly. articles.title: On the Challenges of Using LLMs in High-Risk AI Recruitment: Guiding Questions for Legal Conformity with the AI Act
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.27462v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (AI Act) imposes detailed obligations on providers of high-risk AI systems but offers limited operational guidance, particularly when these systems integrate third-party General-Purpose AI (GPAI) models. articles.title: Trajectories Through Parsons Problems: Making Student Difficulty Patterns Visible to Instructors
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.26799v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing Parsons problem tools primarily focus on correctness, indicating whether a student solved a problem, but providing limited visibility into the underlying problem-solving process. Without that visibility, instructors cannot see which blocks caused repeated confusion or which distractors were consistently selected. articles.title: Explain Your Code: AI-Based Examination at Class Scale
articles.summary: arXiv:2611.26836v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative AI has weakened the link between working code and a student's understanding of it. Oral examination, the traditional test of that understanding, does not scale to large courses. We report the full-course deployment of a three-agent AI system that examines students on their own code. The first, the examiner, asks three questions anchored to specific lines of the submission, adapting difficulty to each answer, in a 16-minute text dialogue.
